title: Weekly phone fast
hookLine: a screen-free stretch; the manna that didn't fall on the seventh day, and two Jewish ways of keeping Shabbat today
tomorrow: a king danced so hard his wife despised him. what did he say?

lines: TWICE AS MUCH ON THE SIXTH DAY.
cards: Ask two Jewish friends whether a phone breaks the Sabbath, and you may get two different answers, both serious. The argument starts in the desert.
Manna falls every morning, bread from heaven, and each family gathers what it needs. On the sixth day they gather twice as much, because tomorrow is a rest.
And still some people go out on the seventh morning with their baskets. The text says they found none.

teach.h: SEE, THE LORD HATH GIVEN YOU THE SABBATH.
teach.b: Moses tells them: "See, for that the LORD hath given you the sabbath." Rest is a gift, and the empty field is part of the gift.
Later the Torah adds: "Ye shall kindle no fire throughout your habitations upon the sabbath day." So here is the debate, and both sides take it seriously.
For Orthodox Jews, Shabbat is kept by its laws, from candle lighting on Friday until the stars come out on Saturday night.

Their rabbis count switching electric devices on or off among the kinds of work Shabbat sets aside. So the phone stays off. The fence is the point: you don't decide each week, so the rest can't be bargained away.
Reform Judaism reads it another way.

teach.h: REFORM: THE SPIRIT, EACH PERSON CHOOSES.
teach.b: The laws serve the spirit of the day, rest and delight and holiness, and each person decides how to keep it. For one family, that means the phones go in a drawer by choice.
For another, it means a long call with a grandmother who lives far away.
One side says: without the fence, rest leaks out. The other says: without the choosing, the day becomes only a rulebook. Under both is the teaching of the manna.
The seventh day is a gift you receive, not a chore you finish. A weekly phone fast can borrow that honestly. It isn't Shabbat.
It's a screen-free stretch, set once and kept, received like the empty field.

how: Orthodox Jews keep Shabbat without using phones or other devices from Friday sundown to Saturday nightfall; some other Jews, and some people of other paths, keep a chosen screen-free stretch each week, with the phone put away in a set place.

o: deleting social apps for good, all at once
a fast from food, kept while scrolling less
a set stretch each week with no screens

games.q: the manna and the Sabbath: tap the pairs.
p: bread from heaven, gathered each morning

s: the Torah names phones as forbidden on the Sabbath
it never mentions them. Orthodox rabbis count switching devices among the kinds of work Shabbat sets aside.
in the manna story, the field was empty on the seventh day
some people went out to gather and found none.
all Jews keep Shabbat in exactly the same way
Orthodox and Reform Jews read the day differently, and both take it seriously.

games.q: one Jewish friend keeps Shabbat with no phone at all. another texts her grandmother every Shabbat afternoon. what's fair to say?
o: both are taking Shabbat seriously, from two real readings of it.
only the first keeps Shabbat; the second just likes a slow day.
the second is right: the old rules were written before phones.
games.why: Orthodox Jews keep the day by its laws, which set devices aside; Reform Judaism leaves how to each person. Both treat the seventh day as a gift.

practice: Put your phone face down in front of you and look at it without picking it up. Decide one screen-free stretch this week, a morning or an evening, and where the phone will sleep while it lasts.
Then let your hands rest open on your knees.

wordCard.voice: Weekly phone fast: a screen-free stretch each week, with a fence around it, borrowed from the Sabbath's gift of rest.

orig.note: Hebrew: Shabbat, the seventh day of rest, from Friday evening to Saturday night.

carryVoice: Hold onto this one: screen-free. The seventh-day field was empty, and that was the gift. Talk soon.
